database.title: DeBoneDiT: Depth-Driven Conditional Bridge Diffusion Transformers for Bone Suppression in Chest X-Ray Images
database.abstract_summary: Chest X-Ray (CXR) is a primary modality for diagnosing pulmonary diseases, yet the overlap of bony structures often obscures critical radiographic findings, increasing the risk of diagnostic uncertainty. While Dual-Energy Subtraction (DES) is the clinical benchmark for bone suppression, its widespread adoption is primarily hindered by specialized hardware requirements and increased radiation exposure. Recently, diffusion-based generative models have shown promise for this task, yet they are still constrained by reconstruction-biased latent compression, prior-induced domain gap, and a scarcity of high-quality paired datasets. To address these challenges, we propose DeBoneDiT, a depth-driven conditional bridge diffusion Transformer architecture for efficient high-resolution bone suppression. We first introduce Depth Auto-Encoder (DAE), a structure-aware vision tokenizer for latent compression. By incorporating a multi-level depth feature loss derived from the pretrained Depth Anything V2 encoder, DAE preserves both visual fidelity and structural consistency. Second, we formulate bone suppression as a source-conditioned Brownian bridge diffusion process, leveraging CXRs as both the diffusion prior and structural guidance to narrow the source-to-target domain gap and maintain anatomical plausibility. Furthermore, we have constructed and released SZCH-X-Rays, the largest publicly available high-quality paired dataset for bone suppression to date, comprising 741 pairs of CXR and DES soft tissue images. Extensive experiments and downstream evaluation demonstrate that DeBoneDiT achieves superior bone suppression performance with reduced computational overhead.

database.abstract_summary: Accurate nuclei segmentation underpins quantitative computational pathology, yet remains challenging due to morphological variability, weak boundaries, nuclear crowding, and pronounced domain shifts arising from differences in tissue preparation, staining, and acquisition. While deep learning and recent foundation models have improved segmentation performance under matched distributions with the original training data, their generalization across heterogeneous histopathology domains remains limited. We introduce GDBA-Net, a parameter-efficient nuclei segmentation framework built around the proposed Gated Dual-Branch Adapter (GDBA). GDBA-Net adapts a frozen SAM2 encoder by integrating pretrained semantic representations with explicit frequency-derived structural priors. The complementary representations are independently transformed through Grid MLP branches and dynamically integrated using sample-adaptive channel-wise gating, selectively emphasizing structural cues relevant to nuclear delineation. Despite using only 4.3 million trainable parameters, GDBA-Net achieves state-of-the-art in-dataset performance and consistently superior cross-dataset generalization across six diverse nuclei segmentation benchmarks under fully supervised, cross-dataset, and five-shot adaptation protocols, outperforming competing CNN-, transformer-, and foundation model based methods. Comprehensive ablations confirm that these gains arise from the coordinated design of semantic-frequency complementarity and adaptive gating rather than increased model capacity. By uniting transferable semantic representations with explicit structural priors, GDBA-Net provides a robust, annotation-efficient solution to domain variability in nuclei segmentation. https://github.com/biplabpoudel25/GDBA_Net

database.title: Non-Abelian quantum Hall states at strong Landau level mixing: finding anyons with first-principles AI
database.abstract_summary: Non-Abelian anyons, strange particles forming the basis of fault-tolerant topological quantum computing, are predicted to emerge in fractional quantum Hall states at even-denominator filling factors. Identifying which topological order is realized has proven to be a challenging problem that requires an accurate, non-perturbative treatment of realistic Landau level mixing, which has so far been missing from theoretical studies. Here we present the first complete solution of non-Abelian quantum Hall problem that includes all electrons and all Landau levels, for spin-polarized electrons at filling factor $\nu = 3/2$. We develop a momentum-resolved neural-network variational wave function, optimized solely on the microscopic Hamiltonian, which gives direct access to the topologically degenerate ground states. Without any physics input about the expected outcome, it discovers a degenerate ground-state manifold whose entanglement reveals anyons with quantum dimension $\sqrt{2}$, the hallmark of Ising-type non-Abelian order. By directly computing the overlap with trial wave functions, we further show that Landau level mixing favors the anti-Pfaffian over other candidate states. Our results demonstrate the power of neural-network wave functions in finding and characterizing non-Abelian anyons from first principles, in regimes of strong Landau level mixing, relevant to many recent experiments.

database.title: Imaging-anchored Multiomics in Cardiovascular Disease: Integrating Cardiac Imaging, Bulk, Single-cell, and Spatial Transcriptomics
database.abstract_summary: Cardiovascular disease arises from interactions between inherited risk, molecular programmes, and tissue-scale remodelling that are observed clinically through imaging. Health systems now routinely generate large volumes of cardiac MRI, CT and echocardiography together with bulk, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, yet these data are still analysed in separate pipelines. This review examines joint representations that link cardiac imaging phenotypes to transcriptomic and spatially resolved molecular states. An imaging-anchored perspective is adopted in which echocardiography, cardiac MRI and CT define a spatial phenotype of the heart, and bulk, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics provide cell-type- and location-specific molecular context. The biological and technical characteristics of these modalities are first summarised, and representation-learning strategies for each are outlined. Multimodal fusion approaches are reviewed, with emphasis on handling missing data, limited sample size, and batch effects. Finally, integrative pipelines for radiogenomics, spatial molecular alignment, and image-based prediction of gene expression are discussed, together with common failure modes, practical considerations, and open challenges. Spatial multiomics of human myocardium and atherosclerotic plaque, single-cell and spatial foundation models, and multimodal medical foundation models are collectively bringing imaging-anchored multiomics closer to large-scale cardiovascular translation.

database.title: Selective Prediction Forgetting for Adaptation of Weakly Supervised Localization of Histology Images
database.abstract_summary: Under strong cross-domain shifts, weakly supervised object localization (WSOL) models often lose their capacity to discriminate and develop a strong prediction bias toward a subset of classes. As a result, the majority of target samples are assigned to these dominant classes. Since source-free (unsupervised) domain adaptation (SFDA) methods typically rely on pseudo-labels, inaccurate pseudo-label estimation causes suboptimal adaptation and poor classification and localization performance. This issue is particularly challenging in computational histopathology, where shifts in organ-specific morphology, staining protocols, and acquisition conditions can significantly impact class-discriminative visual cues. This paper introduces SFDA with selective prediction forgetting (SFDA-SPF), a method designed to mitigate excessive concentration of predictions for dominant classes during target-domain adaptation. SFDA-SPF identifies prediction-dominant classes based on the model's target predictions and selectively revises uncertain samples assigned to them. Importantly, this procedure does not require knowledge of the true target class distribution. In contrast with previous SFDA methods, SFDA-SPF introduces a 'forget set' composed of uncertain samples from dominant classes near their decision boundaries, enabling the classification boundaries to shift away from biased predictions. A second 'retain set' is used to anchor certain and accurate samples. To forget the predictions of dominant classes, SFDA-SPF introduces a complementary optimization objective that reduces their probability while allowing alternative class assignments to emerge. This iterative optimization process reassesses target images for forget and retain sets at regular intervals. In addition to improving image-level pseudo-label estimation, the pixel-level classifier is jointly optimized, further enhancing localization.

database.title: STREAM: Stochastic Riemannian Flow Matching with Anisotropic Decoder for Digital Histopathology Image Generation
database.abstract_summary: Synthetic histopathology image generation addresses patient-privacy concerns and the growing data demands of foundation models. Existing state-of-the-art histopathology generative models use pretrained Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) as conditioning signals. We show this yields conditioning-dominated diversity: on TCGA-BRCA, 62-75% of their output diversity is attributable to the conditioning signal rather than the learned latent space, while de novo synthesis still requires a VFM at inference. We instead use histopathology VFMs as the latent space itself: their patch tokens are $\ell_2$-normalized on the unit hypersphere $\mathcal{S}^{d-1}$ with strong angular dominance and intrinsic curvature, motivating a Riemannian formulation. We present STREAM, the first framework to apply Riemannian flow matching in the histopathology domain, in two stages: 1) a bridge-type stochastic perturbation that establishes per-token rectifiability on $\mathcal{S}^{d-1}$ for training a Diffusion Transformer, and 2) a novel decoder training design whose noise covariance is anisotropic in the left-singular basis of the per-token tangent-projected velocity-field Jacobian, spending a large robustness budget on its low-response directions and a small one on its high-response directions. Across TCGA-BRCA and TCGA-COADREAD, STREAM achieves state-of-the-art gFID and ranks first on nearly all histopathology-specific metrics as well. Code and a public gallery of generated images are available at https://chokevin8.github.io/STREAM-Patho/.

database.abstract_summary: Weak bag-level labels are widely available in computational pathology, whereas reliable instance-level annotations for whole-slide images remain expensive and ambiguous. Weakly supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) achieves strong bag-level classification, but instance-level supervision from attention scores, model predictions, negative bags, or spatial refinement may fail to identify class-specific local evidence. We propose ProtoPur, a prototype-purity pseudo-labeling method for weakly supervised instance-level learning in pathology whole-slide images. ProtoPur estimates class-balanced local purity over prototype regions constructed from frozen foundation-model features, and assigns pseudo-labels to high-purity regions strongly associated with a target class. This purity-first design separates class-specific evidence from negative or shared morphology, with coverage used only to ensure sufficient pseudo-label assignment. We provide a PAC-style analysis showing that the risk of an instance classifier trained with ProtoPur pseudo-labels can be decomposed into a standard uniform-convergence term and a ProtoPur-specific pseudo-label noise term, comprising selected-region mismatch and a coverage residual. Experiments on three public whole-slide image datasets with two pathology foundation encoders show that ProtoPur consistently improves instance-level performance across multiple MIL backbones while maintaining competitive bag-level performance. Pseudo-label quality comparisons on two public datasets further demonstrate that prototype-purity selection provides stronger instance supervision. These results suggest that the foundation-model features contain exploitable instance-level supervision signals, and ProtoPur is a way to reveal and use these signals from weak bag labels without requiring dense instance annotations.

database.title: Medical Imaging Classification with Cold-Atom Reservoir Computing using Auto-Encoders and Surrogate-Driven Training
database.abstract_summary: We introduce a hybrid quantum-classical pipeline, based on neutral-atom reservoir computing, for medical image classification, focusing on the binary classification task of polyp detection. To deal effectively with the high dimensionality, we integrate a guided auto-encoder. This pipeline learns compact and discriminative representations of image data that are also well-suited for quantum reservoir computing. A key challenge in such systems is the non-differentiable nature of quantum measurements, which creates a 'gradient barrier' for standard training. We overcome this barrier by incorporating a differentiable surrogate model that emulates the quantum layer, enabling end-to-end backpropagation through the entire system. This guided training process is jointly optimized for classification accuracy and for faithful image recovery from the auto-encoder. The learned latent representations are encoded as pulse detuning parameters within a Rydberg Hamiltonian, and quantum embeddings are subsequently obtained through expectation values. These embeddings are then passed to a linear classifier. Our simulations show that this method outperforms some traditional approaches that use PCA or unguided autoencoders. We also conduct ablation studies to assess the impact of various quantum and training parameters, demonstrating the robustness and flexibility of our proposed pipeline for real-world medical imaging applications, even in the current NISQ era.

database.abstract_summary: Histopathology classifiers must transfer across acquisition sites while exposing evidence that can be checked independently. Evidence Field couples learned image measurements and spatial classification with a native covering-program record. We evaluate this architecture on all 455,954 released CAMELYON17-WILDS patches, using patient-separated source partitions and two held-out hospital centres. Eighteen from-scratch fits compare four Evidence Field objectives with residual convolutional and compact vision-transformer classifiers. Checkpoints, temperatures and review thresholds are selected using source validation. The source-selected paired-cross-entropy ensemble achieves areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.9356 and 0.9453, with accuracies of 84.46% and 86.77% at the two held-out centres. Corresponding convolutional values are 0.7352 and 0.7656, and transformer values are 0.8502 and 0.7924. Evidence Field has 10,550 trainable parameters per member and additionally returns selected covers, signed region and interaction terms, contextual dependencies and independently reconstructible predictions. Patient-cluster intervals, calibration, source-fixed review policies and recorded training resources characterize the results. A 340-image, three-member audit reconstructs probability mixtures and 6,120 class programs under three rigid views. The evaluation supports cross-centre discrimination and reproducible computation for these implemented models; unequal family tuning, previously examined public targets and limited patient groups constrain broader interpretation.

database.title: Spatiotemporal Adaptive Eigenspectrum Remapping in Transcranial Ultrasound Localization Microscopy
database.abstract_summary: Clutter suppression is a critical preprocessing step in ultrasound blood flow imaging, yet conventional singular value decomposition (SVD) filtering depends on data-specific eigenvalue cutoffs that can remove slow flow along with tissue clutter. Here, we introduce adaptive eigenspectrum remapping (AER), a general framework in which clutter is suppressed by continuously remapping, rather than truncating, the eigenvalue spectrum of the spatiotemporal covariance, and we investigate zero-phase component analysis (ZCA) matrix whitening as an instance of AER for transcranial ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM). Rather than discarding eigenspaces, ZCA-based AER whitens the eigenvalue spectrum, reducing the dominance of coherent clutter, including skull reverberation, while retaining weak flow signals. We evaluate AER on both temporal and spatial covariance matrices in mouse brain datasets acquired with long temporal ensembles. Compared with SVD filtering, ZCA improves microbubble contrast and vascular image quality, increases trajectory density across low- and high-concentration regimes, and reveals more low-velocity trajectories in ULM velocity maps. Spatial AER further maintains reconstruction quality across extended ensembles and enables fuller single capillary reporter (SCaRe) reconstructions, including connected artery-to-capillary-to-vein tracks. These results support AER, here instantiated as ZCA whitening, as a data-adaptive alternative to manually thresholded SVD filtering for high-resolution microvascular imaging.

database.title: Image Moment Estimation for Crowded Datasets
database.abstract_summary: Single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is an imaging technique capable of reconstructing high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) structure of biological macromolecules from a set of noisy projection images taken at random viewing directions. The mathematical model for cryo-EM images typically assumes that each image contains exactly one particle, which is centered at the origin. However, many experimental datasets contain particle images which include multiple particles: one central particle and a few crowding particles. This deviation from the model leads to inaccurate estimation of image statistics, such as the low-order image moments. To account for this, we propose a method to estimate image moments while correcting for the effect of crowding particles. This method can be run directly from a set of cryo-EM micrographs with picked particles, and we demonstrate its efficacy on a wide array of synthetic data.

database.abstract_summary: High-fidelity 3D generative modeling underpins game asset creation, medical imaging, and VR/AR environmental design, where geometric structure directly influences perception and decision-making. Diffusion models represent a powerful paradigm for point cloud generation. However, existing approaches rely heavily on local voxel or patch features and often miss global structural organization, and much less work has studied how global conditioning can be used to improve generation quality. In this paper, we introduce HilbertGen-3D, a novel topology-aware conditional diffusion framework based on Hilbert-Multifractal Conditioning (HMC). HMC computes multi-scale voxel measures, serializes them via a 3D Hilbert curve to expose structured spatial dependencies, and estimates the generalized fractal dimensions from scale-dependent partition functions. We encode these signals as global embeddings and multi-scale tokens, and inject them into a diffusion denoiser through an efficient bottleneck fusion module. Across the Chair, Airplane, and Car categories of ShapeNet, our two conditioning variants reduce the absolute deviation of 1-Nearest Neighbor Accuracy (1-NNA) from 50% by up to 8.90 percentage points and increase coverage by up to 5.88 percentage points relative to TopoDiT-3D. This shows that combining local density cues with global Hilbert-multifractal structure provides a simple and effective recipe for high-fidelity and diverse 3D generation.

# shixuanli01/HMC-DiT3D
**Stars**: 0 | **Language**: Python
**Description**: HMC-DiT3D is a research project focused on generating 3D point clouds of shapes using a diffusion transformer (DiT) model. It incorporates a novel 'Hilbert-multifractal condition' (HMC) to guide the generation process. The HMC involves voxelizing point clouds at different scales, serializing these voxel measures along a 3D Hilbert curve, and then summarizing their multifractal statistics. A windowed transformer encodes these sequences into conditioning tokens, which are then fed into the DiT denoiser via a bottleneck resampler. The conditioning can be provided by either a learned VAE or a library of real data samples. The repository includes code for HMC extraction, the DiT-3D model, data loading, training, evaluation metrics, and generation scripts. It also provides installation instructions and details on building an exact Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) metric.

database.abstract_summary: Optical pooled screens connect genetic perturbations to changes in cell morphology and behavior, but turning the microscopy data into interpretable results takes complex, multi-day analyses. Established pipelines process this data, yet researchers still select parameters, inspect outputs, and resolve failures for each experiment. Here, we present Brieflow-auto, a pipeline-specific harness implemented as a Claude Code plugin that lets a coding large language model (LLM) operate Brieflow, an open-source end-to-end pipeline for optical pooled screening data. A researcher supplies experimental facts and approves the launch. An agent tunes parameters in an interactive notebook, and the harness validates the configuration, monitors execution, recovers from common failures, and checks output quality. For pipeline defects, the agent opens upstream issues proposing backward-compatible fixes for the broader community. In five previously analyzed screens, harness runs yielded more cells with a confident single-gene assignment than the original hand analyses. On a screen the pipeline was not designed for, the harness turned each failure into a reviewed upstream fix. More broadly, we propose that wrapping an established pipeline in a harness can substantially accelerate its use and the long-term reliability of its codebase.

database.title: Learning the Shared Latent Structure of Cryo-EM Inverse Problems
database.abstract_summary: Understanding biomolecular function requires characterizing three-dimensional structure and conformational variability, for which cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is a powerful tool. Cryo-EM produces noisy two-dimensional particle images in which molecular structure, particle pose, and imaging conditions are jointly encoded. Recovering biological information from these observations spans inverse problems including pose estimation, heterogeneity analysis, and reconstruction. These tasks are usually addressed independently despite shared protein structure and image formation, motivating a common representation across inverse problems. Since biologically meaningful differences may be spatially localized, we study self-distillation with complementary global and masked patch objectives. Because experimental dataset discrimination can reflect acquisition-specific cues, we develop controlled synthetic and experimental evaluations and find that structural discrimination benefits from dense spatial features. We introduce the EMber family of vision transformers, pre-trained on >50 million experimental particle images from 214 EMPIAR datasets together with simulated projections from 268,000 molecular assemblies. EMber improves upon existing methods at conformational and compositional discrimination by 14.85 and 14.26 percentage points, estimates conformational populations to within 1.59pp error with a linear probe, and produces particle assignments yielding reference-quality reconstructions in fewer epochs. We demonstrate how to learn representations that capture biological information for use across multiple cryo-EM inverse problems.

database.title: CRUX: Clinical-Text Anchoring for Cross-Institutional CT-Pathology Fusion in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Survival Prediction
database.abstract_summary: Accurate prognosis in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) benefits from integrating computed tomography (CT) and histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), which capture complementary macroscopic and microscopic disease characteristics. Fusing these modalities is difficult: their features come from different pretrained foundation-model encoders and lack spatial correspondence, and both are sensitive to institution-specific acquisition and staining, causing multimodal models to overfit site-specific artifacts and generalize poorly. We present CRUX (CRoss-modal Unification via teXt anchoring), a fusion framework that uses clinical text---encoded by a biomedical language model---as an institution-invariant semantic anchor. Because clinical variables follow standardized classification systems, their embeddings occupy a representation space that is consistent across institutions, providing a stable reference frame for aligning heterogeneous imaging features. CRUX introduces a text-mediated cross-modal bridge in which CT- and pathology-derived text-query summaries exchange information within a compact text semantic space through a learnable hub token, avoiding direct image-space cross-attention that would propagate domain-specific artifacts. We evaluate on 2,157 NSCLC patients from five hospitals, holding out one hospital (N=446) entirely for external validation. CRUX attains an external concordance index (C-index) of 0.761, the highest among all unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal configurations. Notably, direct CT-WSI fusion degrades under distribution shift, whereas text anchoring restores and improves cross-institutional generalization. These results indicate that language-model-encoded clinical text is an effective structured prior for robust, generalizable multimodal cancer prognosis.

database.abstract_summary: Promptable segmentation models turn one 3D bounding box into an instance mask. Box placement therefore limits how fast microscopy volumes with thousands of objects are annotated. Each box must be checked in several synchronized viewers, but napari-bbox shares no state between viewers. An edit must update every viewer and slows down with more boxes. napari-TurboBox instead holds one shared copy of the boxes for all viewers. In a four-viewer layout, napari-TurboBox needs a few milliseconds per mouse move to update the three slice viewers up to $10^4$ boxes. The same update in napari-bbox leaves the 33 ms budget beyond about $10^3$ boxes and takes 159 ms at $10^4$. Boxes stay axis-aligned and export to COCO and YOLO as per-slice 2D boxes. napari-TurboBox is a pure-Python plugin for napari 0.6.6 to 0.9. The code is available at https://github.com/N-Friederich/napari-turbobox under the Apache 2.0 licence, and version 0.1.0 is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23090828 on Zenodo.

# N-Friederich/napari-turbobox
**Stars**: 0 | **Language**: Jupyter Notebook
**Description**: napari-TurboBox is a napari plugin designed for annotating 2D and 3D images using axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs). It features a shared store for all bounding boxes within an annotation, displayed simultaneously across multiple napari viewers (e.g., one editable 2D view and multiple read-only 2D and 3D views). Edits are synchronized in real-time to all connected views. The plugin enforces axis alignment and keeps boxes within image boundaries when the image shape is known. It supports exporting annotations in various formats, including per-slice COCO or YOLO for training machine learning models, as well as native NumPy/JSON formats.

database.title: Evidence Field: Adaptive Covering Programs for Medical Imaging

github.provenance_context: cs> is incorrect. IX-F Public reproduction artifact https://github.com/isararsiddique/evidence-field : code/reader

database.abstract_summary: Medical image classifiers typically return predictions without a native contract for independently reconstructing their spatial decision computation. Evidence Field is a trainable spatial-program architecture that jointly produces class scores, selected covering programs and signed evidence. Its encoder combines absolute and image-relative response fields with associative spatial moments and learned characteristic sums. A typed classifier scores individual regions and parent-conditioned multiplicative groups; a covering recursion selects scale, partition and composition. We establish exact one-fold coverage, optimality within the registered grammar, a bound relating smooth training to hard inference, signed-score conservation and class-centred offset invariance. Direct contractions and their adjoint specify arithmetic and storage scaling on two- and three-dimensional grids. Native output records bind inputs, parameters, supports, types and contextual dependencies to individual and ensemble predictions. In a separately reported histopathology application, patient-separated training and evaluation across held-out centres provide empirical evidence for the architecture. Trained mechanism and corrected-loss comparisons distinguish predictive effects from implementation correctness; independent readers reconstruct descriptors, routes, scores and probability mixtures. The principal contribution is a coupled representation, decision and evidence architecture whose selected computation can be reproduced independently.

database.title: Cross-polarization pairing for label-free few-shot thin-section classification
database.abstract_summary: Few-shot classifiers of rock thin sections are meta-trained on many rock types that a petrographer has identified slide by slide, and this identification is the costly step that new collections lack. We study few-shot recognition of unseen rock types when no training slide is identified, and the only information available is what the microscope records anyway: which slide an image comes from, and whether it was taken in plane-polarized (PPL) or cross-polarized (XPL) light. We first show why generic unsupervised pseudo-tasks fit this setting poorly: the positives they find without labels are either wrong or near-duplicates of the anchor, so they teach the model little. Polarized-light microscopy provides positives that avoid both problems. The PPL and XPL views of one field show the same grains, so they are correct by construction, yet they look very different. We propose cross-polarization pairing (XPP), which treats each slide as a pseudo-class and pairs its PPL and XPL views of the same field location, so that matching must rely on grain shape and texture rather than on colour. On the Nanjing University collection of 108 rock types, with support and query images taken from different slides, XPP is the best label-free method on average over three random splits, and matches a supervised model trained on 78 identified rock types. Controls show that colour augmentation and other acquisition positives do not reproduce the gain. We also show that the image-level protocol of earlier work is saturated, and propose a cross-slide protocol in its place.

database.title: Learning from the Right Regions: Class-Conditioned Explanation Guidance for Medical Imaging
database.abstract_summary: Deep neural networks can achieve strong predictive performance in medical imaging while relying on regions unrelated to the predicted finding. Explanation-guided learning can address this problem, but multi-label classification introduces a key challenge: multiple abnormalities may coexist in an image, requiring each prediction to align with its corresponding spatial evidence. We propose a class-conditioned explanation-guided learning framework that constructs a separate explanation for each positive class and penalizes evidence outside its class-specific annotated regions. We instantiate the framework using Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) and evaluate it on 14 abnormalities using EfficientNet-B1, ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, and Swin-B. Explanation guidance substantially improves annotation alignment across all architectures: All-Saliency Precision increases from 0.140 to 0.625, 0.052 to 0.551, 0.060 to 0.403, and 0.095 to 0.570, respectively. These improvements are accompanied by smaller, architecture-dependent changes in classification performance. Our results show that class-conditioned explanation guidance can substantially improve where multi-label classifiers concentrate their explanatory evidence while largely preserving predictive performance.

database.abstract_summary: Tissue graphs represent histology images as graphs over tissue-conforming superpixels, which keeps homogeneous tissue regions intact instead of cutting them into rectangular patches. To embed superpixels, current encoders crop them to bounding boxes and then pad, resize, or mask them, so background or fill values can leak into the node features. This matters in practice, and especially in medical imaging, where a prediction should depend on the tissue and not on an arbitrary preprocessing choice: on BACH, changing only the fill of the masked region shifts the accuracy of frozen encoders by up to 6 percentage points, larger than the differences among the four best encoders under mean fill, and the preferred fill differs between datasets, so it cannot be fixed once and for all. We present TAN (Tissue-Aware Network), a compact convolutional encoder (0.41M parameters) that processes each superpixel at its native shape and extent and excludes background from every operation, which makes its embeddings exactly invariant to the fill by construction. Under identical masks and an identical graph classifier, TAN's accuracy on BACH is not significantly different from that of the 303M-parameter foundation model UNI (81.1% vs. 80.7-82.6%, depending on the fill), with ~740x fewer parameters, ~1,190x fewer FLOPs, and no pretraining. On BRACS, TAN is close to a ResNet18 trained under the same protocol and trails the histopathology foundation models. An ablation with TAN's architecture but standard processing of fill-padded crops shows that masking keeps accuracy similar (nominally higher on BACH, lower on BRACS, within noise) at less than half the FLOPs.

database.title: LithoWorld: An Endpoint World Model for Lithography Process-Window Recovery
database.abstract_summary: Lithography process drift can move a fabricated pattern outside its process window, producing unqualified scanning electron microscopy (SEM) morphology. We present LithoWorld, an endpoint world model for SEM-guided parameter recovery. Interior representative targets jointly determine qualified reference appearance and correction supervision. A causal predictive branch aligns currentimage features with endpoint representations, while a conditional flow policy generates a two-dimensional correction as an action chunk. The model learns from 173 groups of measured SEMs organized as focus-exposure maps, preserving unmeasured cells as unknown. On 200 test pairs from the 73-group subset, LithoWorld achieves 88.5% qualified-region success and 46.0% interior success, exceeding the strongest comparison method by 2.5 and 6.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablations separate the effects of target selection, endpoint alignment, and output parameterization. Qualitative SEM retrieval illustrates recovery to qualified interiors without requiring exact reference-coordinate matching.

database.abstract_summary: Deep learning has achieved strong performance in computational pathology, but explaining whole-slide image (WSI) predictions remains challenging. Existing explanation methods often highlight important regions without identifying their morphological patterns, leaving a gap between patch-level computational evidence and slide-level pathological interpretation. We propose ProtoGTX, a graph-based framework that combines spatial contextualization with a flexible morphological prototype vocabulary. ProtoGTX separates the reference prototypes used to define morphological concepts from the predictive model: the reference vocabulary can be generated from training data by unsupervised clustering or supplied externally, and remains fixed during classifier training. Patch features are first contextualized over a spatial graph, after which learnable prototypes representing morphological concepts are optimized through cross-attention. Their slide-level activation profile is aligned with the morphological composition induced by the fixed reference prototype bank. On the CPTAC and BRACS datasets, ProtoGTX outperforms the evaluated MIL, prototype-based, and graph-based baselines, with particularly pronounced improvements on BRACS. Qualitative analyses further show that spatial contextualization transforms fragmented patch-level prototype assignments into more coherent tissue regions. In BRACS, prototype maps also co-localize with pathologist annotations and regions relevant to slide-level prediction. These results demonstrate that ProtoGTX provides complementary semantic and spatial explanations while retaining a prototype vocabulary that can be defined independently of the predictive model. Code is available at https://github.com/mizuno-group/ProtoGTX.

database.abstract_summary: Medical vision language models have demonstrated strong potential for medical image understanding and reasoning. However, their interpretability and reliability remain limited because medical vision language tasks require precise visual grounding and clinically coherent explanations. This is particularly challenging due to complex imaging patterns and scarce expert annotations. These challenges reduce the effectiveness of conventional reasoning methods and lead to visual hallucination, defined as the generation of text that is not grounded in the given visual input, which further limits their applicability in clinical practice. To mitigate these challenges, we propose an interpretable medical inference (I$^2$-Med) framework that enhances visual faithfulness during inference without additional training to improve reasoning and explanation faithfulness in medical vision language models. During text generation, I$^2$-Med uses a visual guidance module to check whether each candidate word is supported by the medical image and consistent with the current reasoning. Based on this guidance, the model's output scores are adjusted to favor visually grounded words, without changing the model parameters. Extensive experiments on the OmniMedVQA benchmark, covering eight medical imaging modalities and five clinical question types, demonstrate that our proposed I$^2$-Med framework generates more clinically meaningful and visually faithful reasoning chains and reduces visual hallucination under standard medical VQA evaluation metrics. The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/mtanveer1/l2-med}.

database.title: Junction Geometry Survives an Unidentifiable Blur
database.abstract_summary: Thin filaments cross in microscopy, and dispersed spectra cross on X-ray detectors. At a junction, where these structures cross or branch, how many straight arms meet, and which way do they go? Unknown blur obscures the answer. At a balanced crossing, distinct Gaussian blurs can even produce the same observation law. We show that the arms can still be recovered. For separated rays of nonvanishing weight and an unknown centered Gaussian-mixture blur, a distance combining arm count, directions, relative weights and supporting lines is bounded by a constant times the Euclidean difference in cell probabilities on a sufficiently fine fixed grid. The bound is uniform over a bounded model class, including unidentifiable blurs. From $n$ positions or photon counts, the minimax error is of order $n^{-1/2}$. This rate is proved for a global estimator. In practice we fit rays and blur by constrained local likelihood, reducing the BIC count when two detectors agree on fewer arms in the microscopy studies. Across three studies with protocols fixed before evaluation, on 360 crossings and branches assembled from measured single-molecule localizations, the fit gets the arm count and every direction within $10^\circ$ 24 to 37 percentage points more often than a tuned fixed-scale Hessian ridge detector, averaged over 25 to 400 localizations. On acute angles with correct counts, mean absolute error is $3.5^\circ$ to $4.3^\circ$, versus $10.4^\circ$ to $15.5^\circ$. On Chandra spectra, 38 of 90 fits at 800 photons find all four arms within $10^\circ$; among these, median error is $0.023^\circ$.

database.abstract_summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer binary clinical questions with a yes or no token, leaving the decision threshold implicit and fixed. We derive a continuous score from a single forward pass by renormalizing the probabilities of the yes and no tokens, allowing the threshold to be adapted to clinical needs without retraining. We evaluated this approach with MedGemma and Gemma-3 (4B and 27B) on six medical imaging datasets. The default threshold was frequently misaligned with the task: for identifying normal chest radiographs, MedGemma-27B labeled every image as abnormal, whereas a validation-selected threshold yielded a sensitivity of 0.945 and a specificity of 0.696. Normalization achieved the highest AUROC on four of six datasets (CheXpert: 0.819 vs. 0.777 for raw and 0.743 for text-elicited probabilities), and a single decision required 53-79 ms on one GPU. This simple post-hoc method turns medical MLLMs into fast classifiers with adjustable operating points. Code: https://github.com/TruhnLab/llm-threshold-calibration

database.abstract_summary: Technical artifacts introduced during tissue preparation or slide scanning remain a major obstacle to developing robust computational pathology algorithms for hematoxylin and eosin (HE)-stained whole-slide images (WSIs). Despite the growing number of quality-control tools, their real-world utility remains hard to assess because of the limited number of publicly available implementations and the lack of systematic, multi-dataset comparisons. This paper presents a benchmark of artifact segmentation methods for HE-stained WSIs. After a literature review, six publicly available algorithms were selected and compared in terms of their ability to segment artifact-free tissue and selected artifact classes. Two publicly available datasets and a newly introduced dataset released to support further research were used for evaluation. Tissue samples from multiple medical centers and different organs are included, enabling evaluation across heterogeneous data sources. Segmentation performance was assessed using Dice Index, pixel-level recall, and false discovery rate for artifact-free tissue segmentation. For algorithms supporting multiclass artifact segmentation, class-wise Dice Index and inter-class misclassification were evaluated. In addition to segmentation quality, processing time was assessed. Statistical analysis revealed significant differences in segmentation performance between methods. HistoKit, which incorporates a modified version of the GrandQC, was identified as the best-performing algorithm, while HistoQC was the worst. In terms of artifact types, dark spots and out of focus regions were harder to segment than others. Finally, a simple post-processing step was introduced for HistoKit, which further improved segmentation performance. The benchmark establishes a reference for evaluating and developing artifact segmentation methods for HE-stained WSIs.

database.title: Dynamic self-ensemble on multi-exit residual vision transformer for small-data image classification
database.abstract_summary: Vision Transformer (ViT) has garnered increased attention for image classification in recent years. However, ViT is notorious for its data-hungry problem as it achieves high-performance results when only trained on large-size datasets. In this paper, we study how ViT specifically works on small-scale datasets with limited data where the availability of image data is often constrained in practice, especially in fields such as medical imaging. To mitigate the issue, we designed a multi-stage residual ViT, dubbed ReSEViT, with the self-ensemble method to utilize multi-level information from intermediate features. Due to the complex decision boundaries for classifications, relying on a single classifier can lead to prediction errors. Hence, we propose a new learning method for ViT, named self-ensemble learning, which ensembles multi-stage classifiers in a single model. Our self-ensemble comprises a novel approach, Dynamic Learner Selection (DLS), to adaptively select the importance of different stages. ReSEViT incorporates residual token embeddings which is a ResNet-like block to model effective local structures alongside with transformer blocks in each stage. The integration of residual tokens and self-ensemble learning into a multi-stage ViT highlights the reduction in redundancy, prediction error and variance while maintaining an efficient model size for small-scale image datasets.

database.title: Reliability-Preserving Compression for Deployable Medical Image Segmentation
database.abstract_summary: Post-training compression of pretrained medical segmentation models commonly uses quantization, pruning, or distillation to reduce model size and computational cost. Existing medical segmentation quantization studies mainly evaluate Dice, model size, memory, and latency, but this is incomplete for safety-critical use because compressed models should also preserve uncertainty signals that indicate unreliable predictions. We study this problem in compressed MRI/CT segmentation and formalize why Dice can remain stable while uncertainty changes. Motivated by this failure mode, we propose score-guided aggregate-validated mixed precision (SGAV-MP), a post-training compression framework that selects layer precisions under reliability constraints. SGAV-MP ranks quantization actions with a compact benefit-risk score and accepts them only after full-model reliability validation on a calibration set. Across five 2D backbones and three 3D benchmarks, SGAV-MP preserves FP32-level Dice and high uncertainty-map agreement, achieving $3.59\times$--$7.8\times$ compression in 2D and $4.73\times$--$7.82\times$ in 3D. We also report backend-supported TensorRT deployment measurements separately to distinguish runtime execution from reliability-preserving storage compression.

database.abstract_summary: To determine where computation is needed in volumetric segmentation networks, we analyze block-level redundancy and stage-wise token-mixer contribution. Centered Kernel Alignment reveals high input-output representational similarity within blocks of representative convolutional, hybrid, and Transformer-style segmentation networks. Similarity-guided pruning reduces their parameter counts by 39-75% while decreasing mean Dice by less than 0.4 percentage points. To examine token mixers within blocks, we introduce Anatomical Relation Distortion, which quantifies how bypassing a mixer distorts feature relations between labeled anatomical positions. Applied to an unpruned candidate architecture, Centered Kernel Alignment indicates high representational redundancy in intermediate encoder mixers, whereas Anatomical Relation Distortion shows that they contribute little and the bottleneck mixer most. These findings motivate SlimFormer++, which uses Selective Mixing blocks with windowed Mamba mixing in the first encoder stage and only residual channel MLPs in deeper stages. At the bottleneck, Augmented Mixing injects similarity-weighted sparse long-range context into the axial taps of a depthwise convolution at cost linear in voxel count. Evaluated against 12 baselines across eight public CT, MRI, and ultrasound datasets (1,809 cases), SlimFormer++ achieves the highest mean Dice (87.84%) and lowest mean HD95 (6.50 mm) with the fewest parameters (5.98 million). These results support stage-aware token mixing as a design strategy for improving the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in volumetric segmentation. The source code is available at https://github.com/WHHHHHY822/SlimFormerPlusPlus

database.title: Multi-scale Fusion of Fast Vision Mamba and Foundation Model Features for Patch-Level Gleason Grading in Computational Pathology
database.abstract_summary: Automated Gleason grading of prostate whole slide images (WSIs) enables faster and more consistent cancer risk stratification. However, it remains a challenging task due to the subtle morphological differences between grades, the severe class imbalance arising from rare patterns, and the diagnostic features that span multiple spatial scales. Pathology foundation models (FMs) extract strong patch representations but often operate at a single-scale, which limits spatial context and disproportionately affects classes that depend on broader context. The challenge of fusing multiple scales and complementary models, with minimal data and computational resources, remains unresolved. We propose a multi-scale classifier built on state-space models. Our method combines two complementary feature sources: a frozen foundation model, and a lightweight FastVim, pre-trained on ImageNet and distilled from the foundation model, that reads the raw image crops. At each scale, a Mamba model encodes the features from both sources with linear-time spatial context, and a jointly trained head fuses the encoded representations into one prediction. On the PANDA dataset, our method reaches macro F1 of 0.894 and Gleason 5 F1 of 0.802 under 5-fold cross-validation, a 12% and 21% relative improvement over the best single-scale model. A controlled study over 5 foundation models, 5 base classifiers and 3 scales confirms that the gain holds across encoders, with larger improvements observed at smaller scales.

database.title: On the Benefits of Uncertainty Estimation for Species Classification: A Case Study on Optimizing Expert re-Annotation
database.abstract_summary: Automated identification of diatoms from microscopic images is a cornerstone of large-scale freshwater biomonitoring, yet the high diversity of species and strong class imbalance pose significant challenges for reliable classification. In this study, we develop a ResNet-18 baseline for a 759-class diatom dataset and investigate how calibrated confidence estimates support selective classification to reduce expert workload without sacrificing taxonomic integrity. While the initial model exhibits overconfidence with an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 0.117, post-hoc temperature scaling (T = 2.12) dramatically improves reliability, lowering the ECE to 0.055.By leveraging these calibrated probabilities within a triage framework, we demonstrate that a Selective Macro-F1 score of 99.01% can be maintained at 66.2% coverage (rejection threshold $\tau$ = 0.934). Qualitative analysis reveals that the system effectively functions as an intelligent filter, consistently deferring rare taxa-such as AAMB and AASI-and ambiguous morphologies for expert review. Our findings, supported by the torch-uncertainty framework, highlight the potential of simple calibration techniques to make automated diatom identification practical and robust, prioritizing the preservation of rare species metrics essential for ecological assessment. To support reproducibility, our code, environment specifications, and calibration results are available anonymously at https://anonymous.4open. science/r/greenprwksp-B53D/README.

database.title: XGLASS: X-Ray, Gaze and Language Assisted Slice Sequencing for CT Volumes

github.provenance_context: \times less time and 10.9 × \times less GPU memory per finding, supporting its use as a lightweight slice selector for volumetric CT analysis. The code and pretrained checkpoint are available on GitHub . <div i

database.abstract_summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve remarkable performance on 2D medical images, such as X-rays or pathology images, while 3D VLMs that directly process CT/MRI volumes lag behind due to limited 3D training data and the predominance of 2D foundation architectures. To leverage powerful 2D VLMs for analyzing medical volumes, which contain hundreds of slices, it is therefore necessary to focus only on those few slices, which are diagnostically relevant. To enable such a prioritization, we propose XGLASS, a method that transfers medical expertise from 2D X-rays to 3D CT for task-aware slice prioritization. XGLASS uses disease-conditioned importance maps derived from language-aligned radiologist gaze on X-rays and spatially aligns them with coronal CT projections, bringing gaze priors and CT content into a shared 2D representation. The fused gaze-prior/CT projection is then used to predict a disease-specific ordering of axial slices, prioritizing diagnostically relevant slices. XGLASS significantly improves budgeted retrieval over 2D and 3D-native baselines, achieving a top-10 hit rate up to 75.9% for the best-performing disease. In practice, this means that after inspecting only the top 10 slices (4.17% of a 240-slice scan), XGLASS identifies a diagnostically relevant slice in more than 75% of cases. For downstream slice-wise finding classification, an XGLASS-selected 30-slice candidate set reduces model calls by 87.5% while improving F1 by 11.3 percentage points over all-slice inference, 4.2 points over the strongest 2D selector, and remains competitive with 3D-native selectors while requiring up to 130.8 times less time and 10.9 times less GPU memory per finding, supporting its use as a lightweight preselector for volumetric CT analysis. The code and pretrained checkpoint are available on https://github.com/michaelgloeckler/XGLASS.

database.title: Localization Gains from Explanation Regularization Should Not Be Interpreted as Faithfulness Gains.
database.abstract_summary: Training-time explanation regularization is often evaluated by whether saliency maps become more concentrated within annotated regions. We argue that this criterion alone is insufficient: transformation consistency, lesion localization, and faithfulness to the classifier are distinct properties and should be evaluated separately, particularly in medical imaging. We examine this distinction through a case study of Contrastive Grad-CAM Consistency (CGC) in three-class brain tumor MRI classification. Using a single-channel ResNet-50 with five-fold patient-grouped cross-validation, we compare a cross-entropy baseline with CGC. CGC changes overall Pointing Game (PG) from $27.24\%$ to $36.02\%$ and Relevance Mass Accuracy (RMA) from $11.17\%$ to $18.01\%$, while classification accuracy changes from $93.63\%$ to $94.87\%$. Perturbation-based faithfulness metrics show inconsistent changes: Insertion Area Under the Curve (IAUC) changes from $0.73$ to $0.78$, whereas Deletion Area Under the Curve (DAUC) favors the baseline ($0.36$ versus $0.41$; lower is better), and overall Iterative Removal Of Features (IROF) is $0.57$ for both models. These results support our position that improved spatial agreement with pathology should not be interpreted as a general improvement in explanation faithfulness. We therefore recommend property-specific evaluation in which the property targeted by the explanation objective, spatial agreement with reference regions, and model reliance are measured and reported separately.

database.title: 3D Diffusion Models for Medical Imaging
database.abstract_summary: Generative deep learning methods such as Variational Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks or Diffusion Models have achieved remarkable results in image synthesis. In particular, Diffusion Models have demonstrated superior image fidelity and sample diversity compared to other approaches on standard benchmarks, while also offering more flexible training dynamics as evidenced both in natural image domains and in medical applications. In medical imaging including Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Positron Emission Tomography, such models have various important use-cases including data augmentation, domain transfer, image reconstruction, inpainting, image augmentation and artifact correction. Further, generated images can be conditioned on patient characteristics, medical reports, segmentation masks or other images. Specific challenges arise due to the 3D volumetric nature of medical images, which translate to substantial demands in terms of memory, compute, and training data. This article provides a comparative overview of 3D Diffusion Models which have been developed for medical images, with a focus on current performance, limitations, and an outlook for future work.

database.title: Scaling Vision Foundation Models for Toxicologic Pathology
database.abstract_summary: Here, we present TOX-FM, a family of non-clinical PFMs trained on large-scale diverse histopathology datasets of over one million whole slide images consisting of over 60 organs across six animal species from over 14,000 toxicology studies across six decades. We introduce a comprehensive benchmark of 18 non-clinical downstream tasks, incorporate an established benchmark of 9 clinical downstream tasks, and evaluate TOX-FM against state-of-the-art clinical PFMs across both non-clinical and clinical domains. Notably, we explore open questions surrounding domain-specific training and cross-domain generalization, offering insights into the opportunities and challenges of applying PFMs in the non-clinical domain.

database.title: What Language Adds, and at What Cost: Four Controlled Probes of Pathology Vision-Language Models
database.abstract_summary: Vision--language models (VLMs) promise to make computational pathology queryable and able to draft reports, but how much language adds beyond the vision backbone is unclear, because almost every system is evaluated by its developers on test sets of their own choosing. We grade published evidence by how it was produced and test four claims with controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Report text adds prognostic signal: adding a frozen embedding of the stage-redacted report to a slide embedding raises the pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and by 0.016 for overall survival across 1{,}633 TCGA patients, and restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable accuracy at inference: with features and pooling fixed, zero-shot classification is statistically indistinguishable from a supervised linear probe for lung and renal cancer subtyping. Slide-level question answering is barely grounded: SlideChat answers 74.82\% of SlideBench-VQA(TCGA) items correctly with the slide and 74.41\% without it, whereas its language backbone alone reaches 43.52\%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8--23\% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language. Language thus adds real but narrow value, and we propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.

database.abstract_summary: Differential privacy (DP)'s effect in medical imaging is typically evaluated only through end-to-end performance, leaving the mechanism of privacy-induced utility loss unclear. We introduce Differential Privacy Representation Geometry for Medical Imaging (DP-RGMI), a framework that interprets DP as a structured transformation of representation space and decomposes performance degradation into encoder geometry and task-head utilization. Geometry is quantified by representation displacement from initialization and spectral effective dimension, while utilization is measured as the gap between linear-probe and end-to-end utility. Across over 594,000 images from four chest X-ray datasets and multiple pretrained initializations, we show that DP is consistently associated with a utilization gap even when linear separability is largely preserved. At the same time, displacement and spectral dimension exhibit non-monotonic, initialization- and dataset-dependent reshaping, indicating that DP alters representation anisotropy rather than uniformly collapsing features. Correlation analysis reveals that the association between end-to-end performance and utilization is robust across datasets but can vary by initialization, while geometric quantities capture additional prior- and dataset-conditioned variation. These findings position DP-RGMI as a reproducible framework for diagnosing privacy-induced failure modes and informing privacy model selection.

database.title: Shifting Adaptation from Weight Space to Memory Space: A Memory-Augmented Agent for Medical Image Segmentation
database.abstract_summary: Medical image segmentation is fundamental to clinical workflows, yet models trained on a single dataset often fail to generalize across institutions, scanners, or patient populations. While vision foundation models have shown great promise in addressing this challenge, their deployment typically requires task-specific fine-tuning, which introduces substantial communication overhead in federated learning and prevents continuous knowledge evolution during deployment. In this work, we propose a memory-augmented segmentation agent (MemSeg-Agent) that shifts adaptation from weight space to memory space, enabling few-shot learning, federated supervised learning, and test-time adaptation within a unified architecture. MemSeg-Agent conditions a fixed backbone with lightweight static, few-shot, and test-time working memories, which are dynamically composed by an agentic controller. In federated settings, we update compact memory units instead of model parameters, substantially reducing communication overhead. Experiments on four public datasets demonstrate strong performance and robustness to domain shift: Static memory alone matches or surpasses strong supervised baselines with high parameter efficiency, and test-time working memory further improves in-domain and cross-domain performance without fine-tuning. Overall, MemSeg-Agent introduces a new paradigm for scalable and adaptive medical image segmentation in the era of agentic AI.

database.title: Pathway-Structured Privileged Distillation for Deployable Computational Pathology
database.abstract_summary: Integrating transcriptomics and histopathology can improve cancer risk modelling, yet practical use is constrained by the limited availability of RNA profiling in routine settings. Here we introduce Mixture of Pathway Experts (MoPE), a knowledge-distillation framework that reframes multimodal learning as privileged distillation for histology-only inference. MoPE is motivated by the partial observability between RNA profiles and whole-slide images: histology can capture morphology-linked consequences of certain molecular programmes, but cannot be expected to reconstruct the full transcriptomic state. MoPE encodes RNA-derived pathways and transfers the molecular supervision to pathway-indexed pathology experts through memory-usage alignment. Across diverse public benchmarks and two independent breast cancer cohorts, MoPE consistently improved WSI-only inference performance relative to baseline methods. Pathway-usage analyses and human-audited visual inspection provide bounded inspection of model behaviour and candidate morphology-linked readouts. These results support pathway-structured privileged distillation as a promising route to using molecular information during training while preserving RNA-free inference.

database.title: MergeSurv: Merging-Based Continual Learning for Survival Analysis on Whole-Slide Images
database.abstract_summary: Survival analysis on Whole Slide Images (WSIs) is important in computational pathology for prognosis estimation and treatment planning. However, existing survival models are typically trained independently for each cancer cohort, making continual adaptation computationally expensive for gigapixel-scale WSIs. In this study, we propose MergeSurv, a merging-based continual learning framework for WSI survival analysis. A pathology vision-language foundation model is independently fine-tuned on each task, and the learned parameters are sequentially merged into a unified model without storing previous training data. We further investigate two inference strategies: One-for-All (OFA) and Voting-Expert Aggregation (VEA). Experiments on four TCGA cohorts demonstrate that MergeSurv outperforms naive fine-tuning as well as representative regularization-based and rehearsal-based continual learning methods, while effectively reducing catastrophic forgetting. The results suggest that model merging is a promising direction for scalable and privacy-preserving continual learning in computational pathology.

database.title: DoAtlas-2: A Foundation for Self-Evolving Causal Biomedical Discovery
database.abstract_summary: We introduce DoAtlas-2, a foundation for self-evolving causal biomedical discovery that organizes knowledge around causal mechanisms and advances through external evidence from human populations. DoAtlas-2 integrates 771 research resources covering more than 720,000 participants in 48 countries, from longitudinal clinical phenotypes, medical imaging, and continuous physiological signals to eight molecular layers, together with an evidence network of approximately 4.7 million literature-derived records over 93,566 concepts and 149,383 candidate causal relations. DoAtlas-2 autonomously formulates research questions from evidence gaps and unresolved mechanisms, prespecifies their causal designs, and generates validated analyses. Supporting, challenging, and unresolved results continuously revise mechanistic interpretations, the causal evidence state, and the discovery frontier, so that DoAtlas-2 self-evolves within a closed loop of hypothesis generation, empirical testing, and renewed discovery. DoAtlas-2 has systematically evaluated 2,031 research questions. In the Human Phenotype Project (HPP), it formulated 4,014 candidate pathway questions across vascular, early-glycemic, and hepatic-metabolic systems, and screening of the first 1,079 yielded statistical support for 756. Representative studies identify blood pressure as a convergence node linking adiposity, hepatic, and lipid phenotypes to vascular outcomes, and show that an adiposity-inflammation-blood-pressure pathway is largely attenuated by joint adjustment for body mass index (BMI) and smoking. The discovered vascular network constitutes a completely interpretable predictive foundation, admitting exact attribution of every prediction and closed-form mediation effects. DoAtlas-2 thereby unifies causal mechanism discovery, population-evidence testing, and interpretable prediction within one continuously evolving foundation.

database.title: Certified Abstention for Provably-Unidentifiable Index-Phase Recovery in Image Registration
database.abstract_summary: Image registration underpins measurement across scanning, camera, and microscopy imaging, yet a fundamental question is rarely posed: when is the sample-to-position map recoverable at all, and when does any estimator that reports a position necessarily fabricate one? We show that in reference-perturbed sampled imaging, where samples are localized through a perturbed reference, position fidelity (where samples land) and phase fidelity (which reference index becomes each block's origin) are logically independent: no policy acting on position information alone can guarantee phase fidelity. We derive a tight resolution threshold separating recoverable from provably-unidentifiable registration, and a recovery framework that certifies identifiable regions--recovering them exactly--while abstaining on provably-unidentifiable regions rather than hallucinating structure. On a deployed scanning system we measure a direction-bimodal registration offset consistent with the theory. Against classical and learned restoration baselines, certificate-free offset estimators fabricate structure on the unidentifiable regime, whereas the certified method abstains rather than fabricating. Finally, the certified-abstention mechanism carries across scanning, rolling-shutter, and cryo-electron-microscopy imaging--declining rather than fabricating on the regime it flags--though how completely it abstains and how tightly it bounds kept-region risk stay modality-specific (at extreme SNR the cryo-EM certificate abstains only partially): a structural-versus-statistical boundary in registration reliability.

database.title: Diffusion Posterior Sampling with Uncertain Forward Models
database.abstract_summary: Diffusion posterior samplers reconstruct signals by combining a pretrained diffusion prior with a measurement likelihood specified by a forward model and a noise model. Calibration and reference data can characterize uncertainty in the forward model's parameters, such as blur kernels or detector responses. Fixing these parameters at estimated values leaves their uncertainty out of the likelihood, and parameter errors are thus absorbed into the reconstruction. We introduce an uncertainty-aware likelihood (UAL), a Gaussian approximation to the marginal likelihood obtained by integrating over the uncertain parameters. For each candidate signal, UAL propagates parameter uncertainty into a structured measurement covariance, reducing the quadratic penalty along residual directions that parameter variation can explain. Existing samplers can use UAL in their data updates while retaining their pretrained diffusion priors and sampling schedules. Under a fixed Gaussian nuisance model, we bound likelihood error from linearization and average divergence between the exact marginal and UAL posteriors. We compare samplers with and without UAL across six inverse problems spanning Gaussian and motion deblurring, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and fluorescence microscopy, and find improvements in reconstruction and ensemble prediction. UAL reduces geometric mean MSE by 9% to 20% across samplers in the main Gaussian-deblurring setting and by 51% to 92% in motion deblurring when non-blind samplers use the population-mean kernel. In motion deblurring, DAPS and PnP-DM with UAL also give 6.2 to 6.4 dB higher ensemble-mean PSNR than published BlindDPS and Fast Diffusion EM. On the ablation set, UAL outperforms trace-matched isotropic inflation for PnP-DM in both deblurring tasks; in motion deblurring, it also exceeds the best-tested fixed scalar data weighting by 3.3 dB for PnP-DM and 4.2 dB for DAPS in average PSNR.

database.title: Spatially Informed and Direction Sensitive Representation Learning for Spatial Transcriptomics
database.abstract_summary: Cellular states are shaped by both intrinsic gene expression programs and the spatial microenvironment in which cells reside. Spatial transcriptomics makes this context measurable, but effective representation learning requires capturing both spatially informative molecular signals and intercellular organization. Existing approaches address these challenges only partially: conventional gene selection can overlook spatially structured signals, while methods for encoding cell-cell relationships often either reduce a cell's microenvironment to proximity alone, discarding direction, or rely on absolute coordinates tied to an arbitrary tissue frame. Consequently, cells with similar neighbor distances but distinct spatial organization may receive overly similar representations, despite experiencing different biological contexts that shape their cellular states. We introduce Tessera, a spatial representation learning framework that addresses both molecular selection and cellular context. Tessera combines spatially informed gene selection with a geometric inductive bias that contextualizes each cell within its local tissue environment. By modeling relative cell-cell relationships, Tessera is translation-invariant while preserving direction, allowing neighboring cells to contribute differently according to their spatial context and cellular state. Across held-out tissues and technologies, Tessera outperforms existing spatial foundation models in representation quality and generalizes zero-shot to contexts up to $16\times$ larger than those seen during training.

database.abstract_summary: Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end-to-end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine-tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine-tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state-of-the-art foundation model pre-trained on substantially more data. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region-specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open-source package on https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.
